video_title: Why Elon Wants to Put Data Centers in Space
gist: Planetary VC investor Romez argues the AI buildout's binding constraint is not chips but grid interconnection — poles and wires — which is why capital is flooding into behind-the-meter gas, batteries, and frontier siting like Elon's orbital data centers and Thiel-backed floating ocean data centers (Pontthalasa), all of which are fundamentally regulatory arbitrage. He is a rare West Coast skeptic of general superintelligence, arguing AI only becomes superhuman in formally verifiable domains and that proprietary, experimentally generated data — not model architecture — is the real moat.

themes.theme: Grid interconnection as the binding AI constraint

insights.claim: AI scaling laws require doubling compute for merely linear performance gains, forcing power demand growth at a pace the US grid has no recent experience delivering.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: Compute demand is structurally super-linear in energy, so power infrastructure — not model labs — is the durable scarcity to own.
insights.quote: It means you have to keep doubling the amount of compute to get linear gains in AI performance.

insights.claim: The US grid grew 5-7% a year in the 1950s but has had roughly zero growth for the last two decades, making poles and wires — not chips — the bottleneck on AI buildout.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: Two decades of atrophied buildout capacity means transmission, interconnection and equipment suppliers face demand shocks they cannot quickly absorb — pricing power for incumbents.
insights.quote: In the ' 50s, we built out the grid 5 7% growth a year, but for the last two decades, it's been zero growth.

insights.claim: Chip production is running at roughly twice the pace at which new load can be hooked up to the grid, and a new grid interconnection request now carries a five to seven year wait versus being routine a few years ago.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: A 2:1 mismatch between silicon supply and interconnect capacity implies persistent premium pricing for any asset that shortens time-to-power.
insights.quote: Chip production is about twice the pace that we can hook things up to the grid and that's the bottleneck everyone is trying to work around.

insights.claim: A data center generates roughly $20-40 of revenue per $1 it spends on electricity, which is why operators rationally pay far above grid rates for onsite generation just to shorten time-to-power.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: Energy is a rounding error against AI revenue, so speed-to-energization — not cents per kWh — is the variable to underwrite in any power or data center investment.
insights.quote: if you look at the cost of electricity going into a data center versus the revenue it generates, it generates 2030 $40 of revenue per dollar it spends on energy

insights.claim: Contrary to public perception, the US regions with the greatest data center buildout generally have lower electricity prices that have not risen, but utility commission rate rules still block data center builders from simply paying for grid upgrades without cost pass-through.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: The political backlash narrative is factually weak, and the real unlock is a regulatory fix at state utility commissions — a catalyst to watch state by state.
insights.quote: places where we've seen the greatest data center buildout in general have lower electricity prices in the country and have not seen them go up

insights.claim: Large gas turbines from manufacturers like GE are sold out five to seven years, pushing data center developers toward small turbines a tenth to a twentieth the size mounted on semi-tractor trailers.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: Demand is being forced down-market into modular/mobile generation — a supply gap that favors small-turbine and trailer-mounted power vendors over the sold-out majors.
insights.quote: the big turbines made by companies like GE are sold out 5 to seven years

insights.claim: Boom Supersonic has pivoted from building a supersonic jet to repurposing its engine as a behind-the-meter power plant for data centers, within roughly the last six months.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: Turbine scarcity is pulling aerospace propulsion companies into power generation — a template for repricing any firm with turbomachinery IP.
insights.quote: Boom Supersonic was trying to build a supersonic jet a few years ago or as recently as six months ago. They've pivoted to taking their engine and making it a power plant uh for behind the meter power for data centers.

insights.claim: Batteries installed at a data center that charge overnight and avoid touching the grid during peak afternoon hours exploit the fact that transmission is only fully loaded a few hours a day, and recent regulatory changes have just enabled this.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: Storage converts existing underused wires into new interconnect capacity — the cheapest way to buy time-to-power and a direct tailwind for grid-scale battery vendors.
insights.quote: We build the grid out for peak demand for, you know, late afternoon in the summer when the AC is on. But most hours of the day, the poles and wires, which again are the bottleneck, are not loaded.

insights.claim: About a third of data centers expected to be built this year use cobbled-together onsite generation, possibly as many as half next year, but the approach forces a 30-50% overbuild for spare capacity.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: A 30-50% overbuild requirement means generator and switchgear demand runs well above nameplate data center capacity — size supplier TAM accordingly.
insights.quote: About a third of data centers uh that we think will get built this year are doing some version of that. Maybe as many as half next year

insights.claim: Colossus one probably exceeded its air permits and drew lawsuits, and the noise complaints attributed to data centers actually come from the behind-the-meter generators, which confines the DIY generator model largely to rural sites.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: Permitting and nuisance litigation are the real cap on generator-hacked capacity, steering siting toward remote land and raising the value of rural powered land.
insights.quote: data centers themselves are quiet, but these generators behind the meter are really loud

insights.claim: Despite the rush to onsite generation, essentially every data center ultimately wants a grid connection because no operator wants to run its own power plant.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: Behind-the-meter generation is a bridge asset, not a terminal state — beware underwriting onsite power as a permanent business model.
insights.quote: I think almost every data center really wants to have a grid connection ultimately. Nobody wants to manage their own power plant.

themes.theme: Orbital data center economics and the Starship bet

insights.claim: Orbital data centers require launch costs to fall by a factor of four to ten from current levels before space compute can compete with ground-based costs.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete, trackable threshold for when space compute becomes investable — watch $/kg to orbit against a 4-10x reduction.
insights.quote: you've got to bring launch costs down by somewhere between a factor of four and a factor of 10 from where they are now to compete against costs on the ground

insights.claim: Hitting the launch cost needed for orbital compute requires full two-stage reusability — catching both the upper and lower stages — plus a cadence of multiple Starship launches per day.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: Upper-stage recovery and daily cadence are the specific engineering milestones that gate the entire orbital compute thesis.
insights.quote: they've got to be able to launch a lot of Starships. They've got, you got to get to the point of launching Starship multiple times per day for that launch cost to get cheap enough.

insights.claim: Orbital data centers are best understood as the demand-side business model that finally justifies Starship's fleet size and launch cadence, exactly as Starlink was invented to justify launch economics for the Mars ambition.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: Reframes space data centers as a SpaceX financing mechanism rather than a compute product — the strategic reason to expect Musk to push it hard regardless of near-term unit economics.
insights.quote: Elon originally wanted to go to Mars. He didn't want to build a satellite telecoms network. He built Starlink because it was the business model that worked for launch.

insights.claim: The guest explicitly rejects the argument that compute demand will exhaust viable ground siting and force a move to orbit, saying there are many other places to put compute on Earth.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: A key bear case against space-compute valuations: the scarcity premium underpinning them may never materialize.
insights.quote: Now, I don't actually buy that argument. I think there's a lot of other places we can figure out to put compute.

insights.claim: Covering the world's deserts with solar plus batteries is likely cheaper than orbit until Starship reaches scale, and baseload solar-plus-storage projects in the UAE and Chile already pencil out cheaper than behind-the-meter gas.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: 24/7 solar-plus-storage undercutting onsite gas is the near-term winning configuration — a concrete signal to favor desert-sited renewables-plus-storage data center plays.
insights.quote: in the UAE in Chile we have solar plus battery projects that are base load solar uh that are cheaper than behind the meter gas

insights.claim: Cooling in space is a solvable mass-and-cost problem — space is an insulator with no convection or conduction, so heat must be dumped via large coated aluminum radiator fins that add launch weight.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: Reduces the widely debated cooling objection to a single variable — launch cost per kg — which is already the gating metric.
insights.quote: space is an insulator. There's no uh you know convective cooling, there's no conductive cooling. You touch space and no heat leaks out.

insights.claim: Maintenance and failure rates, not cooling, are the genuinely unanswered question for orbital data centers, made worse because cooling loops with ammonia, pumps and compressors add moving parts that can break.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: Underwriting space compute means underwriting an unknown hardware failure rate with no servicing path — the risk most models are currently ignoring.
insights.quote: I think the maintenance question is one of the most unanswered.

insights.claim: Elon's orbital design reportedly runs chips about 25 degrees C (50 degrees F) hotter than terrestrial data centers because hotter chips radiate heat more easily, but hotter operation directly increases failure rates.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: Identifies the core unresolved tradeoff in the space design — thermal efficiency bought with hardware reliability, which could destroy the cost case.
insights.quote: the hotter you run a chip the easier it is to radiate away the heat. Uh but the hotter you run a chip the more failures you have.

insights.claim: Starlink satellites already function as primitive orbital data centers using onboard compute for telecoms, compression and channel hopping, and a satellite carrying a GPU has already been launched.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: Space compute is a continuum already underway rather than a binary future event — early evidence to track before capital markets price it.
insights.quote: a Starlink satellite doing internet is kind of an orbital data center. It's it's using its compute to handle telecoms and compression and channel hopping and so on

themes.theme: Ocean compute and frontier siting as regulatory arbitrage

insights.claim: Pontthalasa, a startup building floating ocean data centers powered by wave motion, recently closed a large round led by Peter Thiel among others, and the guest is an investor.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: Tier-one capital is now underwriting off-grid ocean compute — a signal that frontier siting has crossed from science fiction to venture-fundable.
insights.quote: we just announced a big round of theirs a little while ago led by Peter Theel among others

insights.claim: Pontthalasa's design is a sphere atop a gently tapering 85-metre tube that forces water up through a turbine as ocean swells push it down, delivering 90-95% continuous power output with almost no moving parts.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: A 90%+ capacity factor with minimal moving parts is a far better baseload profile than solar or wind — the specific number that makes the concept underwritable.
insights.quote: you can have 90 92 95% continuous power output from that system with almost no moving parts

insights.claim: Ocean data centers get cooling essentially for free by conducting GPU heat through a heat sink straight into the metal hull and the surrounding cold water, eliminating the need for a cooling loop entirely.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: Removing both the cooling loop capex and its parasitic power load is a direct margin advantage over terrestrial and orbital designs.
insights.quote: the cold ocean waters give you basically cooling for free

insights.claim: Both space-based and ocean-based data centers are fundamentally the same bet — escaping grid limits, local permitting, zoning and community pushback by moving compute to an unregulated frontier with abundant energy.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: The unifying investment thesis for exotic siting is regulatory arbitrage, not physics — so the trade lives or dies on how binding terrestrial permitting stays.
insights.quote: Let's get past the limitations of the grid. Let's get past local permitting and zoning.

insights.claim: Distributed and frontier siting works only for inference, which can run on a single rack or twenty GPUs, while training still demands roughly a gigawatt in one place with high-speed optical interconnect between racks.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: Splits the data center market in two: giant centralized training campuses versus distributable inference capacity — different assets, different siting economics, different investors.
insights.quote: for inference, when you're just asking a question to an AI model, you might be talking to one rack of servers. Might be talking to 20 GPUs at once.

insights.claim: Distributing compute across many nodes makes the failure of any single node non-catastrophic, which is how frontier deployments absorb orbital debris, solar storms and ocean collisions.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: Redundancy-by-distribution is the risk model that makes frontier compute insurable — the underwriting question becomes node cost, not node survival.
insights.quote: if you distribute the compute enough losing one node is not catastrophic

themes.theme: Texas deregulation and distributed home batteries

insights.claim: Base Power's roughly $9-a-month home battery business works because Texas is a deregulated energy market, letting the company become the customer's electricity retailer and arbitrage cheap and expensive power using the customer's house as a small power plant.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: The value is in the retail energy arbitrage, not the hardware — a template for evaluating any distributed storage company's real business model.
insights.quote: they're using that battery to buy and sell power on the grid, to buy power when it's cheap, sell it back when it's expensive, and they become your electricity retailer

insights.claim: Base Power's distributed battery model is only viable in eight US states, with Texas the largest, which caps the addressable market absent regulatory change elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: A hard TAM ceiling of eight states means expansion depends on state-level deregulation — the catalyst to track for any decentralized grid investment.
insights.quote: That business model works in eight US states.

insights.claim: Texas is the number one US state for solar, wind and batteries with no specific policies promoting them, purely because its competitive wholesale and retail markets let the cheapest resources win.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: Renewables leadership is being driven by market structure rather than subsidy, so subsidy-repeal risk is less relevant than market-design risk when picking energy exposure.
insights.quote: Texas is the number one state in the US for solar, wind, and batteries without any specific policies to advance them.

themes.theme: Picks-and-shovels: miners, components and DC architecture

insights.claim: Every Bitcoin miner the guest knows is shifting to AI because they already hold access to power and AI compute earns more dollars per kilowatt hour than Bitcoin.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: Miners should be revalued as energy-access assets rather than crypto plays, and Bitcoin hashrate economics face a structural bid away from the sector.
insights.quote: the Bitcoin miners I know are all shifting to AI ... it's because they have access to power and that is the bottleneck and you just make more dollars per kilowatt hour going into an AI compute than you do in Bitcoin ultimately

insights.claim: Because power is the binding constraint, economic value accrues to whoever can get load hooked up or route around grid limits, not to whoever owns the compute itself.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: A simple allocation rule for the AI trade: own the scarce input — interconnect rights, powered land, generation — rather than the abundant one.
insights.quote: because power is the constraint the you know value flows to what's scarce

insights.claim: Transformers, turbines and switchboards are in acute shortage with multi-year lead times, and the suppliers are often private, family-owned, risk-averse firms reluctant to add assembly lines — though soaring prices are now drawing both incumbent expansion and new entrants.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: The component bottleneck is a genuine picks-and-shovels opening, and the incumbents' reluctance to expand is precisely what leaves room for new entrants to capture the margin.
insights.quote: transformers classically are are in short supply right now

insights.claim: Because solar output and GPU consumption are both DC while the grid is AC, the industry is now exploring entirely DC-based data centers and higher internal voltages to cut copper wiring and simplify assembly.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: An architectural shift to DC and higher voltage would reshuffle winners across power conversion, switchgear and copper demand — a second-order trade off the AI buildout.
insights.quote: we're seeing people talk about entirely DCbased data centers we're seeing people talking about increasing the voltage in a data center because it reduces how much copper wiring you need

insights.claim: Companies like Giga Energy in Texas, which started in Bitcoin mining hardware and moved into powered land and AI infrastructure, illustrate a broader push by supply chain players to vertically integrate the full data center stack.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano (host)
insights.so_what: Vertical integration from hardware into land and development is the emerging playbook — watch for margin expansion in firms that own multiple layers.

insights.claim: The guest is a rare West Coast investor who does not believe a singularity or general artificial superintelligence is imminent, arguing AI is fundamentally capped by the intelligence and noise level present in its training data.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: A framework for discounting AGI-priced valuations: if capability is data-bounded, the terminal value assumptions in frontier lab pricing are too aggressive.
insights.quote: I'm one of the few people in the west coast who doesn't think we're about to hit a singularity and and ASI that just does everything for us magically utopia or dystopia.

insights.claim: By roughly 2028, and possibly already now, models will have been trained on essentially all books, the entire internet and all scientific articles, exhausting the pre-training corpus of human written work.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: A dated deadline for the end of easy scaling — after which competitive advantage shifts entirely to synthetic and proprietary data generation.
insights.quote: maybe 2028 we will have trained off of basically all the books all the internet all the scientific articles

insights.claim: AI becomes genuinely superhuman only in formal, highly verifiable domains such as games, mathematics and to a lesser degree coding, because those allow unlimited self-generated data with 100% reliable right-or-wrong labels.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: A screening test for AI application investments: if the domain lacks a fast, cheap verifier, do not expect superhuman performance or the associated economics.
insights.quote: the places where we see AI become truly super intelligent are these formal domains that we think about as highly verifiable

insights.claim: Messy domains such as writing a novel, running a company, or setting US foreign policy toward Iran resist superintelligence because there is no way to judge correctness quickly across a million simulations.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: Directly undercuts the 'AI runs your company' narrative — bet against broad agentic automation and toward verifiable-domain tooling.
insights.quote: You don't have a way to judge quickly in a million simulations. Did I get the right answer or the wrong answer?

themes.theme: Data moats, open weights and model routing

insights.claim: Most recent AI capability gains come from synthetic data and reinforcement learning rather than raw web scraping — for example translating a code sample into every other programming language to manufacture training data — and this is believed to be the labs' secret sauce.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: Capability progress is now a data-manufacturing problem, shifting spend toward data pipelines and RL infrastructure rather than more scraping.
insights.quote: a lot of the gains are coming from synthetic data and reinforcement learning

insights.claim: The specialist human data generation market is roughly $10 billion a year already, with private startups like Mercor valued at multiple billions for producing expert data for labs and enterprises.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: A concrete market size and comparable for the data-supply layer — an underfollowed segment expected to keep compounding as pre-training data runs out.
insights.quote: we think the sort of uh specialist human data generation market is something like $10 billion a year right now

insights.claim: Claims that AI will cure cancer or double human lifespan are overblown because biological progress requires experimentally derived data, which is why AI companies are partnering with, acquiring, or licensing data from biotech platforms.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: Deflates AI-biotech hype while identifying the real value: biotech companies with proprietary wet-lab data platforms become acquisition and licensing targets.
insights.quote: AI will cure cancer, AI will double the human lifespan or whatnot. These are overblown expectations.

insights.claim: Data, not compute or model architecture, is the binding constraint on AI progress, and the only durable proprietary data advantage may come from generating the data yourself.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: Screen AI investments for owned data-generation loops rather than data access deals, which are one-time and depreciate once sold.
insights.quote: Data is the bottleneck on AI.

insights.claim: New Limit, founded by Coinbase's Brian Armstrong and working on cellular reprogramming and longevity, exemplifies the sustainable moat: an in-house high-speed cell experimentation pipeline whose data improves AI models that in turn direct smarter experiments.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: The experiment-to-data-to-model virtuous cycle is the specific structure to look for when underwriting AI-biotech — and it is described as rare.
insights.quote: that sort of feedback loop or virtuous cycle, that's the real sustainable competitive advantage

insights.claim: Contrary to fears of AI monopolies, there are no obvious network effects in the AI market — nothing like Facebook — so the market stays hypercompetitive and the value accrues to users today.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: Argues against paying monopoly multiples for frontier labs and in favor of AI-consuming businesses that capture the deflationary surplus.
insights.quote: in the AI market overall, there are no obvious network effects. There's no effect like Facebook.

insights.claim: Open-weight releases structurally benefit the fast follower, since a leader releasing freely usable weights is sabotaging its own margins — which is why open weights come mainly from Chinese labs, Google's Gemma, and Nvidia's Nemotron, the latter because Nvidia wants to sell compute.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: Predicts who will and will not open-source: use open-weight releases as a revealed signal that a lab believes it is behind, and expect Nvidia to keep subsidizing openness.
insights.quote: If you believe that you are in the lead, then releasing uh your model in a way that people can use freely or tweak themselves is just sabotaging your own margins.

insights.claim: Model routing startups can both cut token costs and beat any single frontier model by knowing which model to ping and interpolating answers from several, but routing is famously hard and ChatGPT's removal of the model picker in favor of automatic routing was widely disliked.
insights.speaker: Romez (guest, Planetary VC investor)
insights.so_what: Flags a large, largely unbuilt market — but the ChatGPT backlash shows the product must preserve explicit user control and transparency to win.
insights.quote: they can sometimes get results that are better than any single frontier model on its own if they just know uh when to ping which model

insights.claim: Enterprises moved through Q1 from ignoring token spend to actively optimizing it, because AI product usage is user-generated and therefore exposes companies to uncapped compute cost.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano (host)
insights.so_what: Token-efficiency pressure is now industry-wide, capping inference revenue growth per user and creating demand for routing and optimization tooling.
insights.quote: you essentially have uncapped exposure to token price
